title: Healthy Ways to Cope with Stress
organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
content: Coping with stress in a healthy way will make you, the people you care about, and your community stronger. You can support yourself by taking care of your body. Try to eat healthy, well-balanced meals, exercise regularly, get plenty of sleep, and give yourself a break if you feel stressed out. Avoid using drugs and alcohol as coping mechanisms. Make time to unwind. Try to do some other activities you enjoy. Connect with others. Talk with people you trust about your concerns and how you are feeling. Connect with your community- or faith-based organizations. Recognize when you need more help. If stress gets in the way of your daily activities for several days in a row, talk to a psychologist, social worker, or professional counselor.

title: Stress Management and Relief Techniques
content: Stress can be defined as any type of change that causes physical, emotional or psychological strain. Stress is your body's response to anything that requires attention or action. Everyone experiences stress to some degree. The way you respond to stress, however, makes a big difference to your overall well-being. To manage stress effectively, you can try: 1. Keep a daily routine. Having a schedule can make us feel more in control. 2. Get plenty of sleep. Rest restores the body and mind. 3. Connect with others. Share your feelings with friends or family. 4. Eat healthy foods and stay hydrated. 5. Exercise regularly. Even a short walk can boost your mood. 6. Limit exposure to news and social media if it increases your anxiety. 7. Practice breathing exercises or mindfulness. If stress becomes overwhelming or persistent, seek guidance from a doctor or mental health professional.

title: Box Breathing Technique for Anxiety
content: Box breathing, also known as four-square breathing, is a simple relaxation technique that can help reset your breathing pattern, calm your nervous system, and clear your mind. The practice of box breathing involves four simple steps, each lasting for a count of 4 seconds: 1. Inhale: Slowly breathe in through your nose for 4 seconds, feeling your lungs fill with air. 2. Hold: Hold your breath gently for 4 seconds. Avoid tensing your chest or throat. 3. Exhale: Slowly exhale through your mouth for 4 seconds, releasing all the air from your lungs. 4. Hold: Hold your lungs empty for 4 seconds before taking your next breath. Repeat this cycle for 4 to 5 minutes, or until you feel a sense of calm returning.

title: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR)
content: Progressive Muscle Relaxation (PMR) is a deep relaxation technique that involves systematically tensing and then relaxing different muscle groups in your body. This helps you release physical tension and recognize the contrast between tension and relaxation. To practice PMR: 1. Find a quiet, comfortable place to sit or lie down. 2. Take a few deep, slow breaths. 3. Start with your feet. Tense the muscles in your toes and feet by curling them tightly. Hold for 5 seconds, then release completely. Feel the tension flow out. 4. Move up to your calves. Tense the calf muscles, hold for 5 seconds, and release. 5. Continue this pattern up through your thighs, buttocks, stomach, chest, shoulders, neck, and face. Hold each tension for 5 seconds, then relax for 10 seconds. Notice the sensation of warmth and heaviness in your muscles as they relax.

title: The 5-4-3-2-1 Grounding Technique
content: Grounding techniques are helpful tools to bring your focus back to the present moment when you are experiencing anxiety, panic, or overwhelming stress. The 5-4-3-2-1 method engages all five senses: 1. Acknowledge FIVE things you can see around you (e.g., a clock, a plant, a picture). 2. Acknowledge FOUR things you can touch or feel (e.g., the texture of your shirt, the warmth of a mug, the chair supporting you). 3. Acknowledge THREE things you can hear (e.g., traffic outside, wind blowing, the hum of a computer). 4. Acknowledge TWO things you can smell (e.g., coffee brewing, fresh air, soap). 5. Acknowledge ONE thing you can taste (e.g., a mint, water, or the clean taste of your mouth). This sensory check-in interrupts racing thoughts and helps anchor you to your immediate physical environment.

title: Caring for Your Mental Health: Self-Care Practices
content: Self-care means taking time to do things that help you live well and improve both your physical health and mental health. When it comes to your mental health, self-care can help you manage stress, lower your risk of illness, and increase your energy. Here are some tips to get started: 1. Get regular exercise. Just 30 minutes of walking daily can boost your mood. 2. Eat healthy, regular meals and stay hydrated. A balanced diet and plenty of water can improve your energy and focus throughout the day. 3. Prioritize sleep. Stick to a schedule, and make sure you are getting enough sleep. Blue light from screens can make it harder to fall asleep. 4. Try a relaxing activity. Explore relaxation or wellness programs, which may incorporate meditation, muscle relaxation, or breathing exercises. 5. Set goals and priorities. Decide what must get done now and what can wait. Learn to say 'no' to new tasks if you start to feel overwhelmed. 6. Practice gratitude. Remind yourself daily of things you are grateful for. 7. Focus on positivity. Identify and challenge your negative and unhelpful thoughts. 8. Stay connected. Reach out to your friends or family members who can provide emotional support and practical help.

title: When and How to Seek Professional Mental Health Help
content: It is important to know when to seek professional help for your mental health. Consider speaking with a doctor, licensed therapist, or mental health professional if you experience any of the following for more than two weeks: 1. Difficulty sleeping or sleeping too much. 2. Appetite changes that lead to unwanted weight changes. 3. Difficulty getting out of bed due to low mood or energy. 4. Difficulty concentrating or making decisions. 5. Loss of interest in things you usually enjoy. 6. Inability to perform daily tasks or responsibilities. 7. Persistent feelings of worry, fear, or sadness that feel overwhelming. You can find help by contacting your primary care doctor for a referral, contacting your health insurance company for a list of local providers, or searching directories of licensed professional counselors, clinical psychologists, and psychiatrists.

title: Crisis and Support Helpline Resources
organization: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration
content: If you or someone you know is struggling or in crisis, help is available. You are not alone. 1. In the United States: Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. Services are free and confidential. You can also chat online at 988lifeline.org. 2. Crisis Text Line: Text HOME to 741741 to connect with a crisis counselor 24/7. 3. In the United Kingdom: Call 111 to reach NHS mental health services, or call 116 123 to talk to Samaritans. 4. In Canada: Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide Crisis Helpline. 5. International: If you are outside these countries, please contact your local emergency services (like 911, 999, or 112) or go to the nearest hospital emergency room. These resources are confidential, professional, and available to anyone in immediate distress.
